As we do so, there arises in our minds great joy and satisfaction.
They have been born.

I consider it our good fortune that the first part of this *Ajita* reached publication even before two years had passed and was well-received by scholars. Dr. Viśva... (2) In the introduction to this first volume, I have set forth, according to my understanding, what I intended to say regarding the Mātṛkās, the Tantravārttika-Ṭīkā, and the lineages of the tradition of the Śāstra. Here, however, [the following] twelve...
A brief introduction to the subject matter of this distinguished Mīmāṃsā is presented here according to my understanding.
The Mīmāṃsā consists of twelve chapters (*dvādaśalakṣaṇī*)— comprising twelve books— or sixteen chapters (*ṣoḍaśalakṣaṇī*).
The doubt as to whether [the Self] consists of meditation (*dhyānātmikā*) is the reason; the repetition of the final sūtra of the twelfth chapter occurs there.

It is observed in the Vedānta-sūtras that the repetition of a sūtra indicates completion. For this very reason, it has been so conceived here as well. Otherwise, what purpose would the repetition of the final sūtra serve?

Because the inquiry [into Brahman] has not yet been completed; furthermore, almost all the subjects useful for determining the meaning of Vedic sentences are observed to be contained within the twelve chapters [of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā-sūtra]. In the four chapters constituting the Saṅkarṣa-kāṇḍa, having observed that certain Vedic sentences cannot have their meanings determined by the principles previously investigated, those [principles] useful for determining them [are presented].
The logical principles (*nyāya*) have been described. Here, there is no fixed order; rather, because the subjects are intermingled, it is named *Saṃkarṣa* (the Interwoven).
Herein, there are two thousand seven hundred and forty-four sūtras.
They exist. In each chapter there are four sections (*pādas*), though sometimes there are even eight sections in a chapter;

indeed, that chapter is known by the name *Śarabhapāda*, because a specific bird named *śarabha* has eight legs. Furthermore, each individual section (*pāda*) is divided into topical discussions (*adhikaraṇas*).

First, the subject matter of the dispute attains the status of being denoted by the term *adhikaraṇa* (topic) here. For the purpose of resolving the dispute, five constituent parts have been determined as the method (*prakriyā*) in this context: the connection (*saṅgati*), the subject matter (*viṣaya*), the doubt (*saṃśaya*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The subject matter,
the point of contention, the prima facie argument, and likewise the final conclusion.

"And the connection (saṅgati)—thus the five-membered *adhikaraṇa* is remembered in the treatise. This verse is indeed well-known. [It appears] in Mādhava’s *Jaiminīyanyāyamālā* and Maṇḍanamiśra’s *Mīmāṃsānukramaṇikā*.
Furthermore, these [sections] are extremely helpful for the comprehension of the *adhikaraṇas*, *pādas*, and *adhyāyas*. It has been stated right here:
"Dharma is to be expounded by means of the twelve chapters (*lakṣaṇas*);
therein are those known as *pramāṇa*, *bheda*, *śeṣatva*, *prayukti*, and *krama*."

(3) Authority, extended application, general rule, and specific rule; modification, annulment, common ritual procedure, and incidental application have been set forth in their proper sequence.

In this context, it has been stated that *dharma* is to be elucidated by means of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in this twelve-part Mīmāṃsā. For this very reason, the desire to know arises as to what *dharma* is, what its characteristics are, and what its means of accomplishment are. The intended meaning of the statement "it is to be elucidated by means of characteristics" is that the comprehension of the subject matter occurs through a concise method, and not by any other means.

It is possible. That by which the true nature of an object is understood constitutes its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), for the characteristic of a definition is indeed the possession of properties that distinguish it from others.
I believe there was debate at that time regarding two thousand points. Therefore, [the term] "two-thousand..."
The *ṇyadhikaraṇas* have been set forth by Mādhava, who is renowned for his scholarship, in his *Jaiminīyanyāyamālā*.
In ancient times, almost all people had mastered the *karmakāṇḍa* through the lineage of their gurus; [they were] the sacrifice—

They were indeed the leaders in rituals such as sacrifices; for this very reason, by following the *Dharmasūtras* and other texts, they engaged in their respective duties and attained the state of having fulfilled their obligations (*kṛtakṛtyatā*). Later, as knowledge gradually declined among people and the understanding of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) underwent transformation, various disputes arose concerning the ritual section among those of limited knowledge.

He brought forth the Mīmāṃsā Śāstra. At that time, experts in the field deliberated upon those points of contention that existed, resolving them through the systematic method of *adhikaraṇas*. Since the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) proceeds in accordance with Vedic sentences, the determination of the meaning of those sentences is indeed the fruit of this scripture.

For this very reason, this Mīmāṃsā is designated as a "science of sentences" (*vākyaśāstra*). Furthermore, the following verse briefly indicates the method for determining the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of sentences: "The beginning and the conclusion, repetition, novelty, the result, [the purpose, consistency, and the explanation of the rest]."

"Exegetical argument (*arthavāda*) and logical consistency (*upapatti*) are the marks for determining the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Thus, there may indeed be a difference of opinion among the Mīmāṃsakas at times regarding sacrifices and offerings when they are together with the ritualists (*yājñika*s)— those who follow the *Dharmasūtra*s directly and rely upon the traditional performance of sacrifices— concerning the nature of the scripture.
This is understood through study.

In that regard, the inquiry as to what constitutes the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding Dharma was resolved in the first chapter. It was established across its four sections (*pādas*) that the means of valid knowledge here are fourfold: injunction (*vidhi*), explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), traditional law (*smṛti*), and name (*nāmadheya*).

For instance, when there is doubt as to whether a Vedic injunctive statement is a means of valid cognition or not, [the opponent maintains that] the injunctive statement is not a means of valid cognition.

(8) The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because it depends upon the syntactical connection (*saṅgati*) of its constituent parts, it lacks independence. It is the word-meanings themselves, once understood, that lead to the comprehension of the sentence-meaning; there is no such thing as a "sentence-meaning" distinct from the word-meanings. Therefore, just like the words...

The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that even a sentence possesses independence (*nirapekṣatva*) in the communication of its meaning; therefore, there is no occasion for doubt regarding its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). Incidentally, it is here that the eternality (*nityatva*) of both word and meaning, as well as their relationship, and the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedas [are established].

And this has been established: otherwise, because defects such as error and negligence residing in a person could potentially transfer even to his compositions, those works produced by that person would fall into the state of being invalid (*aprāmāṇya*).

A desire for inquiry arises, just as there is an investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, in the systems of Nyāya and other philosophies.

Why, then, is their examination not performed here as well? If it is asked, "Why is there an examination of only the injunctive and other such sentences?", [the answer is: Just as for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception and the rest, their status as valid cognitions—that is, their capacity to produce knowledge that accords with reality—is established by the fact that they possess non-deviation (*avyabhicāritā*) as their cause, so too this is not the case for injunctive sentences, according to the opponents.

It is clearly stated by the opponents who deny the authority of the Vedas that the Vedic injunctive statements (*codanā*) are characterized by deviation and produce false cognition; this is because it is both necessary and appropriate to exert effort in establishing the validity of these injunctive statements. It is precisely for the sake of resolving this dispute that [the following] is primarily addressed.

The commencement of the treatise: Furthermore, for that which is already established, there is no need for proof, as it is not required. Therefore, there is no formal examination of perception and the other means of knowledge here.
Likewise, Vedic statements of arthavāda, distinct from injunctions (vidhi), are also authoritative.

Although it is difficult to include all explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) here, nevertheless, according to the maxim of the "sample from a cooking pot" (*sthālīpulākanyāya*), one such explanatory passage is established here as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The subject of the inquiry is the statement: "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity. Given the doubt as to whether this sentence possesses authority regarding *dharma* or not, [the following is] the injunction prescribing what must be done:

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that only those sentences which have the nature of an action to be performed can possess authority regarding dharma; therefore, arthavāda sentences lack authority because they are solely intent upon describing already established matters.
As for the reply:

although there is no injunction for performance in such sentences as these, nevertheless, another sentence found within that same context is encountered, namely, "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu. It exists therein.

Thus, there is the injunction for the immolation of a goat as something to be performed. And by virtue of being part of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), the sentence "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity" can be interpreted accordingly. Consequently, the meaning established by these two sentences forming a single syntactical unit is this: since Vāyu is the swiftest deity, therefore the immolation of a white goat should be performed for his sake.
"For the sake of swift attainment. And thus, by means of this description of excellence (*prāśastya*), the injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*) functions toward the instigation of the person.

The explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) provides support for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Regarding that which brings about the comprehension of Dharma, it is indeed authoritative;

thus, sentences such as "the Aṣṭakā should be performed" are heard in scripture. Nevertheless, this specific meaning—that this is a Vedic injunction and its object must be carried out—is not directly perceived there. It is precisely for this reason that Smṛti points it out in this manner.

The doubt is as follows: Is Smṛti (tradition) a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that Smṛti is not a valid means of knowledge because Dharma is characterized solely by Vedic injunction (*codanā*), and thus Smṛtis other than the Vedas are unworthy of authority. In response to this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is formulated: Smṛtis possess validity precisely because they are rooted in the Veda; for it is only those matters remembered by the followers of the Veda that appear in the Smṛtis.

They are not composed of anything new; rather, whatever matters were stated scattered throughout the Vedas have all been collected here in the Smṛtis by the authors of the Smṛtis, who are experts in the Vedas, for the benefit of humanity. Thus, their authority is indeed established. Therefore, the Smṛtis ought to be a means of valid knowledge regarding Dharma.

In this sentence, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," the word *udbhid* is the subject of inquiry. Here, a doubt arises: does this word, by the etymological derivation "that by which [something] is split open" (*udbhidyate 'nena*), enjoin an accessory such as a spade or the like, or does it denote a specific sacrifice bearing that name? Is it merely a particular accessory that is being enjoined?

It takes the form of a spade and so forth. For example, regarding the statement "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the word "curd" (*dadhi*) prescribes the quality of curd.
However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that, because words such as *udbhid* lack a well-known conventional meaning—just like the word "curd"—it does not [prescribe] a quality.

Since there is no need for the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the sense of the possessive suffix (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), which is the cause of [the injunction] being a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), it is not tenable that this is a prescription of a quality.

Therefore, it is proper that this word is simply the name of a specific sacrifice. Consequently, the meaning of the sentence culminates in: "One should sacrifice with the sacrifice named *udbhid*. Thus, it has been well said:

"Prescriptive injunctions (vidhi), explanatory passages (arthavāda), traditional law (smṛti), and names (nāmadheya)— thus the first chapter is stated to have four feet concerning the means of valid knowledge."

In the first chapter, it was investigated what the characteristic of *dharma* is; now, the investigation is commenced as to what constitutes *dharma* and which actions bear the designation of *dharma*. Therefore, the differentiation of actions (*karmabheda*) is primarily the subject matter of the second chapter. [The remainder of the discussion proceeds] by way of its introduction (*upodghāta*), its exceptions (*apavāda*), and what is relevantly connected thereto (*tatprasaktānuprasakta*).

In this context, the meaning is secondary. Since it is the primary fruit (*phala*) that must be defined at the occasion of defining the distinctions among ritual acts (*karma*), an investigation into its essential nature, its means of proof, and so forth, is undertaken first by way of an introductory discussion (*upoddhāta*).
Here, a doubt arises: in an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*), is the *apūrva* connected with all the words, or with only one?

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*),

the *apūrva* is connected with all words because it is the result, and because all words are connected with that result; however, [in the final view], the connection of the *apūrva* is with only one word, since one [word] cannot have a connection with many.

Because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating [multiple apūrvas]. Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that a single *apūrva* is conveyed by one word alone, while other words are construed as being subordinate to it. Now, another inquiry arises: "Is the *apūrva* conveyed by one word alone?"

Once [the sacrifice] has been accomplished, what is that "state" (*pada*) by which it is brought about? In this context, it must be an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*) that serves as the subject matter. Regarding the doubt as to whether the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) is first denoted by the nominal word (*nāman-pada*) contained within that injunctive sentence or by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pada*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is expressed by the nominal word alone. For the result [accrues] only from substances and other factors that are already established in their own nature.

The possibility of [substances] being means [to an end] exists; however, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that substances are incapable of accomplishing a result without an action. Therefore, it is the verbal suffix alone, as the denoter of *bhāvanā*, that conveys the *apūrva*, and not the nominal word.
It has been stated that the *apūrva* is made known by the meaning conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*). The *apūrva*.

The inquiry as to why it must be accepted remains active. Regarding the doubt as to whether the *apūrva* exists or not, the position of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) is the negative alternative. His reasoning is that there is no evidence for its existence, since heaven and the like are designated as the fruits [of action] and are perceived as such. For the proponent (*siddhāntin*), however, the position is the affirmative alternative.
For instance, in the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," it is stated that the sacrifice is the means for attaining heaven.
And this status of the sacrifice as a means to heaven must necessarily be postulated in such a way that it remains logically consistent;
for heaven is not accomplished immediately after the completion of the performance of the sacrifice, but rather in the interval between its conclusion and the attainment of heaven.

Something must be postulated that is woven through both and connects them both; otherwise, a sacrifice that has long since perished could not be the cause of heaven occurring immediately after death, because it would be separated by many intervening operations. Therefore, for the sake of the consistency of the relationship between the means and the end as expressed in the injunctive sentence regarding the sacrifice and heaven—

Whatever is postulated, because it cannot be known through any means of valid cognition other than an injunction (*vidhi*), it is given the name "the unprecedented" (*apūrva*). For this very reason, the venerable Śaṅkarācārya stated: "An action, having perished without first producing some unprecedented [result], is not able to bestow a fruit delayed by another time. Therefore, from the action..."
Or, it is explained that there exists some subtle subsequent state of the fruit, or a prior state of the fruit called *apūrva*.
Therefore, in the first quarter (*pāda*) of the second chapter, the *apūrva* and related matters are analyzed by way of an introductory discussion (*upodghāta*).

In connection with this topic, the definitions of *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa*, the nature of *ūha*, and the definitions of the *ṛk* and other [Vedic meters] have been set forth right here. The primary subject of the second pāda is the determination of the differentiation of ritual acts (*karmabheda*).
This is the intended meaning: it has already been established that the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) is expressed by the verbal suffix itself; and likewise...

Furthermore, examples such as *yajati*, *dadāti*, and *juhoti* are found occurring within a single section (*prakaraṇa*) as verbal roots (*dhātu*) that have been fully formed (*niṣpanna*) as finite verbs (*ākhyāta*). Consequently, a doubt arises: do all these finite verbs express distinct, separate actions, or do they express a single action? This is because in all of them, there is only one single verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) which denotes the productive activity (*bhāvanā*).

Therefore, only one *bhāvanā* (efficient force), only one [result], and only one action are asserted by all; nor is there a distinction based on a difference in verbal roots (*dhātu*), because since the root does not denote the *bhāvanā*, it is irrelevant in that regard—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): although the verbal suffix alone is the indicator of the *bhāvanā*, nevertheless, regarding the verbal suffix...

Therefore, because [the verbal roots] are distinct according to their respective *dhātus*, and since many verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) denote the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) only as colored by each specific root, the productive urges of sacrifice (*yāga*), giving (*dāna*), and offering (*homa*) are indeed mutually distinct. In this context, "difference in words" (*śabdāntara*) alone is the cause for the difference in ritual acts (*karmabheda*). Sixfold difference in ritual acts has been set forth; it is for this very reason that—
Six means of proof (*pramāṇa*) arise that indicate a difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*), one of which is "another word" (*śabdāntara*) cited here.
Likewise, repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), name (*saṃjñā*), quality (*guṇa*), and context (*prakriyā*) indicate a difference in ritual action.
An example of a difference in ritual action through repetition is: "He sacrifices the *samidh* [fuel-sticks], he sacrifices to *tanūnapāt*, he sacrifices to *iḍ*."

Regarding the sentence "He sacrifices outside," there arises a doubt as to whether a single action is expressed by the four occurrences of the verb *yajati*, or whether four distinct actions are expressed. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that a single action is expressed; however, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there are four actions because of the employment of the four instances of *yajati*. For if the action were one, the repetition would result in meaninglessness.
The differentiation of actions by number is as follows: "One should sacrifice seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati" is the subject sentence.

Here, the doubt arises: is the prescribed action one alone, or are there seventeen actions? Since the word *ālabheta* (one should sacrifice), which denotes the action, is singular, the action here is one alone, consisting of the immolation of seventeen animals.

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: the ritual consisting of the immolation of animals dedicated to Prajāpati is not a single action.

The subject matters of the [four] chapters are, respectively, extension (*atideśa*), and the exception to extension (*atideśāpavāda*). This is to be determined as follows:

Although the ritual known as the Darśapūrṇamāsa is one because it is a means to a single result, nevertheless, the performance of the Pūrṇamāsa is indeed distinct from the performance of the Darśa; this is clear precisely because of the difference in the time of performance. And thus, due to the difference in time—
Due to the difference in application (*prayoga*), the repetition of the remaining elements of the application must be performed for each triad; this is the illustration of insertion (*āvāpa*).

The subject matter of the twelfth chapter, however, consists of the definitions of incidental application (*prasaṅga*) and so forth. *Prasaṅga* is the occurrence elsewhere of that which has been performed elsewhere.

Thus, there exists a triad of fires denoted by the term "monastery" (vihāra), consisting of the Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇa, and Āhavanīya forms.
Here a doubt arises: are worldly rites performed in this triad of fires, or Vedic rites, or rather both worldly and Vedic rites?

Since the Gārhapatya and other fires are rendered free of expectancy by such direct scriptural injunctions as "they cook the sacrificial oblations on the Gārhapatya," "they cook the Anvāhārya rice on the Dakṣiṇāgni," and "they offer oblations in the Āhavanīya," it is not tenable for these fires to serve a worldly purpose. Therefore, the conclusion regarding the principal subject (tantrinirṇaya) is that the triad of fires exists solely for the sake of Vedic rites such as the Agnihotra.
[The topic] has been reached.

An investigation into the combination [of rites] proceeds here in the third section (pāda). In the eight-night sacrifice, the first day is named Viśvajit; thereafter, the six-day period named Jyotis; and then the eighth day named Abhijit.

In the Viśvajit sacrifice, which is a *prakṛti-yāga* (archetypal rite), the skin of a calf (*vatsatvak*) is prescribed for wearing; and by virtue of the identity of name, "Viśvajit," that same rite is extended (*atideśa*) to the first day of the eight-night sacrifice (*aṣṭarātra*) named Viśvajit, as well as to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
In those cases, a new, unwashed garment (*ahataṃ vāsaḥ*) is prescribed for wearing, and this [Jyotiṣṭoma] is also called "Jyotis."

By parity, it is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) that the calf-skin (*vatsatvac*) is to be worn during the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), which constitutes the second part of the eight-night rite (*aṣṭarātra*). Furthermore, by extended application, it is also obtained that the unwashed skin (*āhatam*) is to be worn during the final part of the eight-night rite, namely that which is called the *abhivīta*. In all these cases, the wearing [of the skin] is obtained solely through extended application based on the name. Here, a doubt arises: should the calf-skin be worn unwashed, or...?
Is there an option (*vikalpa*) that either garment should be worn? Or is it a combination (*samuccaya*) where both should be worn?

Since a garment is more suitable for wearing as an undergarment (*paridhāna*), while calf-skin is more suitable for covering the upper body (*prāvaraṇa*), both should be worn; thus, it is a combination.
Thus, regarding conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), two expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are heard in the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*):
"One who has omitted either the New Moon or the Full Moon sacrifice should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara;
or, one who, being a regular performer of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, omits the New Moon [or Full Moon] sacrifice, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt."

By whatever statement it is asserted that heaven arises from the sacrifice and that the primary rite is assisted by the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, by that very statement it must necessarily be admitted that these [actions], whether they have perished or not perished, possess some capacity for producing their own effects.

It must be admitted that all things possess causal capacity (*śakti*), because there is no commencement of an effect for those things that lack such capacity. Furthermore, in this context, capacity must necessarily be attributed only to past [moments]. Why?
Because, due to universal momentariness, not even a single action persists anywhere.
How could there be a simultaneous operation toward a single result, let alone toward many?

For indeed, whatever action is undertaken is incapable of producing its fruit all at once because it consists of momentary and subtle parts; how much more so, then, for those rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, which possess multiple constituent elements? For when the *pūrṇamāsa* occurs, the *darśa* does not; and when the *darśa* occurs, the *pūrṇamāsa* has long since perished. Thus it is within a single composite whole.

When there is the *āgneya* [offering], then the *āgnīṣomīya* and *upāṃśuyāja* do not exist; when one of those two exists, then the other two are not found. Since there is no distinction [in the result] arising from the mere performance [of an act] due to the absence of conjunction (*sāhitya*), the fruit heard in scripture as being accomplished through conjunction would not be possible if that conjunction were not achieved. Regarding the doctrine of the self (*ātman*): if the self were not all-pervading, then the perception of pleasure and so forth would occur only at that very place where the body is joined with its possessor (the self), and nowhere else. For if we were to perceive any effect of the self outside the body, or if we were to perceive pleasure, pain, and so forth within another body, then we might conclude its omnipresence. However, since the effect is observed only within one's own body, and wherever that [body] moves, it is perceived there in turn— just like the effects belonging to that body— it follows that [the self] is contained within that very body.

Otherwise, the body itself would have to be omnipresent. [61] In every case of the relationship between substance (*dravya*) and action (*karman*), since actions do not arise without a substance, the substance first produces the action; because it provides a visible assistance, it appears for the sake of that [action]. In some instances, the action turns back again.

In some cases, it assists a substance by merely bringing about its own acquisition of existence (*ātmalābha*). When that mere acquisition of existence is observed for it, then, because of the resulting expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*), an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) can be postulated. However, when it becomes free of expectancy through an observed assistance to the substance—such as the production of rice—which serves another purpose, then at that time, no unseen result [is required].

Since there is no occasion for conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), and because the purposefulness of the injunction is established in quite another way, it is not understood that [the act] is a means to an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). ||6||

Those actions by which a substance is not intended to be produced either in its essential form (*svarūpataḥ*) or as a property (*dharmataḥ*), such as the *prayāja* offerings and others, become for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*) because they are primary with respect to their own means of accomplishment. ||7||

Furthermore, those substances by which another substance is produced— such as when fires are obtained or generated through kindling (*ādhāna*), or when officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are consecrated through selection (*varaṇa*),
or when rice grains are [prepared] by threshing, or rice-particles by grinding— are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*),
because the purification of the substance is desired for the sake of a purpose. This applies whether the purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭārtha*) or invisible (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
If it were performed in exactly the same way [as the model sacrifice], then what would be the purpose of the inquiry?

To this it is replied: even in the case of the *prayaṅgu* oblation, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the threshing—which by extension (*atideśa*) is obtained from the model—is to be performed using *vrīhi* grain as the means. Why?
For a substance mentioned in connection with the principal act does not sublate the substance of an auxiliary;
therefore, just as in the case of the clarified butter used for the *prayāja* offerings, there should be no sublation of the rice.
In the final conclusion (siddhānta), however, they are set aside. Why?
Because a substance that serves the primary purpose is also connected with its purificatory rites;
therefore, the *priyaṅgu* grains must be prepared by all [the rites], including the threshing (*hanti*) and so forth.

But surely, even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the threshing is not prompted by the principal act and thus lacks a purpose in the archetype (*prakṛti*) due to its dependence on rice that is not itself prompted by the principal, the threshing would not apply to the rice in the *prayaṅgu* sacrificial pap, as it is not grasped by the principal act. This is not so; for both [the threshing and the rice] are enjoined together. Then it would be as stated, provided that the purpose [of the threshing] is established by another sentence.
At that time, the substance is already acquired; since its visible benefit is accomplished through that [substance], the action also has its purpose established.

Thus, there is no occasion for postulating an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, the scriptural injunction (*vākya*), like the substance, serves a visible purpose by being subservient to the *kratva-pūrva* (the transcendental result of the sacrifice), yet it functions as the means for regulating the performance of the action. ||6||

Regarding the phrase "by means of the *ādhāna*": the form of the *āhavanīya* fire is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action, not the mere physical form of fire; and since that [ritual status] arises from the *ādhāna*, it serves as an example for production (*utpatti*). The author of the *Bhāṣya* will state that they are "performed" or "refined" (*saṃskriyante*) in the context of production; the author of the *Vārttika*, however, will discuss such refinement (*saṃskriyā*) in the third chapter. For the connection with the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) is indeed the same.

When there is a conflict (paplava), a quality that is not possible [in that context] is enjoined; even there, this [quality] is the differentiator, as he will state later regarding the *abhyupetyavāda* (conditional argument):

This is an introduction to the distinction or non-distinction of actions; that is, does one action impel a single *apūrva*, or do all five actions each impel their own *apūrvas*? What is the prima facie position? That there is one *apūrva*. Why?
Moreover: although the meaning of the suffix is the same, it differs according to the difference in the verbal root;

Previously, by that very word, the action was introduced into the cognition;

Just as the word *yajati* (he sacrifices), having been once perceived through direct perception, is not differentiated upon being uttered again because of the recognition that "this is that very same word," so too is its meaning. And just as in this very case, a direct perception that serves to inform one who already knows—even if it is purposeless—is unable to establish it as a different word, so too a repeated hearing does not establish a different meaning. For [mere] purposelessness [does not constitute a difference].

A name is not included within any category of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, those who advocate for valid means of knowledge must accept as authoritative only that which the Veda makes known. Therefore, in this case, if one were to conceive of difference when non-difference has been understood by the Veda through the word "one" (*eka*), it would be as if the Veda itself had been rendered invalid. Moreover, futility (*ānarthakya*) does not constitute a defect when it is understood through a valid means of knowledge; such is the case here.
This too is a possible interpretation: a word, being touched by the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*), while denoting its meaning, is itself grasped as being part of the performance.

Alternatively, the repetition (*abhyāsa*) will serve to indicate frequency and so forth; for in common worldly usage, even in the absence of that [frequency], the distinction between the two is established through the conventional practice of differentiation, even for one who perceives only the difference between the quality (*guṇa*) and the name (*nāmadheya*).

This is explained as follows: it is not useless. For instance, when that which has been mentioned does not differentiate [the action] by its own inherent nature (*svarasa*), then, in the absence of any other purpose, the status of *samit* and so forth as injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*) serves to constitute the meaning of the sentence. However, if it does effect differentiation, then since the thing to be enjoined is already obtained therein, there is no requirement for another thing to be enjoined; thus, they function as names (*nāmadheya*). The verbal suffix first enjoins [the action] by virtue of its capacity for action;

For when the injunctive power of the prescriptive word is drawn away from the meaning of the verbal root, then, because it lacks the capacity to enjoin multiple things, it requires a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the meaning of that root. In all cases where multiple things are prescribed, since it is impossible for the injunctive power (*vidhi-śakti*) to apply to more than one, there arises an expectation that "one [thing] should be restated (*anūdya*). When this occurs, the restriction is made: "that which revolves three times" (*triparivartate*) is what is meant. Indeed, in the *Paśubandha*, *Soma*, *Ekāha*, and *Ahīna* sacrifices, the cognition of difference based on these [criteria] never undergoes sublation.

Therefore, while those individual instances (*vyakti*) are themselves eternal and subject to being manifested, it is their manifestors that differ. Now, one might object:

This is because the application of distinct words and cognitions is established. For, through connection with a single [day], there is the state of being a *ahīna* (a sacrifice lasting one day); from two up to eleven days, prior to twelve, it is an *ahīna*. But that [twelve-day sacrifice] is of a dual nature in every respect. Taking that as its limit, everything up to the thousand-year sacrifice possesses the character of a *satra* (sacrificial session) due to its connection with continuous time, while it possesses the character of an *iṣṭi* (offering) due to its connection with specific oblations; thus it is established. Likewise, if the generalities such as "jyotiṣṭomatva" (the state of being a Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice) and their individual instances (*vyakti*) are absolutely distinct due to differences in place, time, and so forth, even then there is no fault. [This is] by virtue of having the *karaṇa*-body as their object. [Regarding the second chapter,] the deity is indeed already established. "For whichever deity one is offering the oblation, for us two, let there first be only clarified butter."

Regarding the word "yajati" (he sacrifices): the attainment of the *yājyā* verses is already established, and the introduction of the *anuvākyā* verses must be performed according to the *Dāśatayī* collection; thus, there is nothing contradictory. Therefore, even though it is a separate rite (*karmāntara*), its ritual form (*rūpa*) exists, and consequently, we accept that there is a distinction. However, we do not tolerate the view that they are equally primary (*samapradhāna*). Why?

The application [of the suffixes] occurs only in certain cases where there is a distinct designation of the two [meanings], and the result [arises] from those qualified by that; thus, an equivalence [between the two types of suffixes] is not tenable.

For the designation "Darśapūrṇamāsa" denotes a specific sacrifice; therefore, since the fruit belongs to that alone, the others must be its subsidiaries by virtue of their proximity to it. To this, it is replied:
"The well-known is always intended as the qualifier of the unknown."
Therefore, the meaning of the noun is determined in accordance with the requirements of the sacrifice.

In all cases where an action is prescribed by means of a name, because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), sometimes the specific meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is defined by the name, and sometimes the meaning of the name is defined by *yaj*. Whichever of the two has its meaning more firmly established in common usage establishes the other within its own domain. For example, in the expression "by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma," [the name] is defined by the "lights" (*jyotis*), such as the *trivṛt* and so forth.

By means of the name, which has its meaning well-established through the performance of the *stoma* sacrifices, the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is diverted from the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites and established as referring to the *soma* sacrifice.
Likewise, in the expression "in the *rājasūya*," the root *yaj*, which is well-known from the sacrifices under discussion, appears as the referent for the name.

It is led to its own specific domain. Therefore, in this case, there is no established usage whatsoever for the two nominal stems joined in a compound in the dual number as they are presented by the words *darśapūrṇamāsa*, by which the sacrifice (*yajati*) could be understood as having that as its object.

On the other hand, since the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) applies to sacrifice in general, it is restricted to the specific sacrifices under discussion by the governing context (*adhikāra*), and thus it is able to establish the unestablished meaning of the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
This will be explained later. However, since these two [mantras] have not yet been identified, it is not untenable [to speak of them here]; thus it is said:

"If, however, one recites the *yājyā* and recites the *puro’nuvākyā*," this is stated with the intention of not subverting the singular number that has already been established. Therefore, he says: "Or rather, of the two *vārtraghna* mantras. And by those two, when combined—

Because of the offering of the place (*deśasamarpaṇa*), the dual-deity rite dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*) is determined; through the manifestation of its constituent parts, the subordinate status (*aṅgabhāva*) of the two mantras recited at the *manotā* stage is to be determined. As for their application (*niveśa*), it occurs only in certain cases. Because the two designations, "Darśa" and "Pūrṇamāsa," end in the dual number, they are applied separately, each excluding the domain of the other. That...

It is not on account of the context alone that a difference in subject matter is untenable, but rather on account of its own capacity (*svaśakti*). Therefore, the two denotative powers (*abhidhāna*) are applied only to certain [actions] in which that capacity is found, and not to the primary action (*prakṛta*) alone. And because the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) is qualified by that [capacity], it too has that as its object. Consequently, here the root *yaji* does not denote the entire primary sacrifice.

the base and the suffix are complete and capable of qualifying the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).

Even if the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) were to apply to the *āgneya* and other offerings due to their connection with the time denoted by its own meaning, nevertheless, because those [offerings] are many, duality is impossible; thus the word is incapable. There is no basis for a conflict by which, through some commonality of phonemes, one might determine that these two refer to those [other sacrifices] either by the logic of modification of verbal forms (*ākhyāta-vikāra*) or by way of being figurative (*gauṇa*). For in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), the connection with time belongs to the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices which are mutually independent and devoid of subsidiaries, because they are presented in that form. That [position] is not to be accepted, because it is adopted with respect to time. By virtue of the intention to express the complete form, the triad—complete with its constituent parts and mutually accompanied—is joined with a single *paurṇamāsī* and a single *amāvāsyā*. This is because of the restriction that in the very same moment one sacrifice is commenced and brought to completion, the other two are likewise completed. Thus, the triad [is established].

The performance of the triad by way of a single unified procedure (*tantra*) becomes established. However, if one were to follow the original time [of each individual], there would be a separate performance for those [elements] devoid of their subsidiaries; thus, there is a distinction. Now, if this is the case, since the two groups joined with one another constitute a single whole, there is no mutual intention (*vivakṣā*) toward them either—just as there is no requirement for the accompaniment of subsidiaries—just as in the case of the subsidiaries themselves.

At that time, consciousness is thus projected by both the full moon (paurṇamāsī) and the new moon (amāvāsyā), and by the new moon, the full moon; thus there is a contingency for both [rites] in each case. Nor is there a contradiction with the time prescribed by the original injunction (*utpattivākya*), because the performance occurs even then.
For he who performs the new moon rite on the full moon day does not thereby fail to perform the new moon rite on the new moon day.

The same applies to the full-moon day (paurṇamāsī). Nor does the originative injunction (utpattivākya) exclude other times, as its function is exhausted merely by prescribing its own specific time. To this it is replied:
"That whose time is not known, yet whose essential nature is not lost..."
For him, time, being afflicted by external conditions, does not cause harm.

There is excessive complexity [in the view that] there is the origination of what is being carried over (*nudyamāna*), and the origination as well as the mutual connection of what is being enjoined. Because of this fault, the cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) would be connected with the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) as qualified by that [sacrifice], or else it would be connected with the deity Agni as unqualified by that [sacrifice]; thus, there would be no proper connection. Having experienced the difficulty of establishing a mutual relationship [between the sacrifice and the deity], there arises again the difficulty of establishing a relationship with the *paurṇamāsī* (full-moon sacrifice). "Because it is possible, the quality [is connected] with the unprecedented [act]" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 2.2.23); thus, there is the status of being a distinct ritual act (*karmāntaratva*).

And since there is the status of being a distinct ritual act, the non-statement of its form remains as it was, resulting in the character of a restatement (*anuvādatā*). Consequently, by force of necessity, one must resort to the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the singular number and so forth. Furthermore—
Nor does this sentence conclude with the connection to another action;
nor, because its own meaning is incomplete, does it depend upon another sentence.

The statement "it consists of eight potsherds" does not denote a human activity (*puruṣavyāpāra*). Nor is it possible to enjoin merely the activity of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), because that is not of the nature of a specific productive operation (*bhāvanā*). Since a specific human activity must necessarily be postulated there, the inference of a sacrifice (*yāga*) follows; for even when a perceptible [activity] is available, it is not proper to resort to an inferred one.

Nevertheless, even though this conceptualization occurs while the sentence remains incomplete and independent of other sentences, the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) situated in the sentences concerning the full-moon and new-moon sacrifices is simply not present here; thus, it does not obstruct the inference. And once the inference has taken place, because the phrase "one who knows thus" (*ya evaṃ vidvān*) has the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*), it is understood as a mere restatement, especially since there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the action.

In such passages as "That which belongs to Agni is on eight potsherds," this [phrase] "one who knows thus"—which differs from the use of the word *yat* and stands in grammatical apposition with the agent—would, if attached [to the injunction], obstruct the force of the injunction (*vidhi*). As it has been said:
"When connected with a single verb of action, the word *yat* does not obstruct the injunction."
That very same [word], when connected with an agent, performs the function of restating an object already obtained by another [word]. (6)
Since there is an option between performing the sacrifice on the new moon day or on the day of the *sāṃnāyya* herbs,
how could there be a fixed sequence of priority among the preparatory materials?

For when there is a distinction between the ritual acts, because their objects are distinct, there is a combination of the *sāṃnāyya* and the *puroḍāśa*; in that case, the collective preparation (*saṃbharaṇa*) and the designation as "first" and "subsequent" are appropriate, but not otherwise. Furthermore, in the first alternative, since there is yet another [act] following the fourth, the term would have to be "the subsequent ones" (*uttarāṇi*), not "the later ones" (*uttare*). ||7||

"One should sacrifice desiring offspring"—and this is not a connection with any other action. There is an absence of that connection which exists through another action; rather, it is a connection with the verbal root of the action itself. Since the person should perform that visible action, there is no contradiction with the injunction, because it is not a restatement of an already existing activity. However, [the phrase] "he who performs" refers to the agent's engagement...
"When [the action] has already been prompted, the application of the injunction is impossible";
and "nor is there a connection with another action," according to Ānandagiri and Mādhava.

[The Section on the Upāṃśuyāja Sacrifice] Now, by means of three sections, the refutation of the view that [certain passages] are collective restatements (samudāyānuvāda) is undertaken. Regarding this, first, in the case of the injunction "He performs the Upāṃśuyāja sacrifice between [the two offerings]," the entire principle previously stated applies. Why?
The [sacrificer], by necessity, relies upon sacrifices prescribed as having form and associated with Viṣṇu and others,
even though the [Supreme Being] is formless and inwardly united.

In those cases, the suffix -tavya denotes an absolute injunction. In that regard, if this were assumed to be a separate sacrifice, it would follow that there is an ignorance of the ritual form (*rūpa*) and the postulation of another unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, the avoidance of *ajāmi* is understood to apply to each of the offerings individually.
And the mention of the upāṃśuyāja was made because of the fault of the jāmi.

From the correspondence between the opening and the conclusion, and because the introduction of the *ajāmi* (non-repetitive) principle and its application refer to the same subject matter, these very injunctions are understood. For in the intermediate sentences, no such explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) or injunction (*vidhi*) is clearly seen. Furthermore, the purpose of the collective restatement (*samudāyānuvāda*) is indeed [to establish] those [acts] which have been unified in the statement: "One should sacrifice silently on the full moon day."

If there were a connection with time, all [factors] would possess primary importance. Now, one might object: how can that which has *upāṃśu* (whispering) as its quality be described as the "form" (*rūpa*), since it is distinct from the substance and the deity? This is not a fault. In every respect, that by which a sacrifice is distinguished from other sacrifices is precisely what constitutes its form. And it is possible to recognize this sacrifice as having a distinct form through its *upāṃśu* nature.

Thus it is said: "A word of such a kind is not capable [of that]. For if this were assumed to be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) based on a distinction between the meanings of its constituent parts, then—since the word *yāja* ends in the suffix *-ghañ*—it would be grammatically incorrect (*asādhutva*) as long as the *kutva* change (the substitution of *k* for *j*) had not occurred.
However, if it is an unanalyzed name (*nāmadheya*), this consequence does not arise. But even if it is a name, it must necessarily be so... [text continues].

And as it is stated in the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra* (1.4.4), "Another scripture is of the same nature as that," so too in the case of "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a low voice," the conclusion follows the opening statement.
Because the conclusion accords with the opening, there is a single subject matter regarding both redundancy (*jāmitā*) and its absence.
Therefore, since the opening statement pertains to the subject matter, the sentence has the purpose of enjoining that. To some extent...

The injunction regarding the ritual act—"He performs the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice"—is not a restatement (*anu-vāda*) of a composite whole. Why?

Just as in the Vaiśvānara passage, where the numbers eight and so forth— by virtue of the opening and closing statements concerning the twelve potsherds— attain syntactic unity with it and do not achieve the status of independent injunctions, so too here, in the opening of the injunction "This is indeed a repetition," the mention of the defect is required by something being enjoined, serving as the means for removing that defect.

It is understood that this is for the purpose of praise (*stuti*). Since "repetitiousness" (*jāmitā*) occurs when nothing is prescribed in the interval between the two *puroḍāśa* offerings, it is determined that the quality of "removing repetitiousness" (*ajāmikaratva*) belongs to that which will be prescribed in connection with the intervening time; thus, because it is known that the phrase "in the interval" (*upāṃśuyājaṃ antareṇa*) is worthy of praise, [the mention of] Viṣṇu and the others is required for those [offerings].
Because of the mention of praise through the form of the *jāmi* (redundancy), the status of being an injunction is disregarded and its purpose as praise is accepted.

For there is no connection with the intermediate time (*antarālakāla*) in those [passages] connected with Viṣṇu and others, by which an injunction of that [intermediate time], or the redundancy residing therein, could be connected with the redundancy mentioned at the beginning as something required for the sake of praise. This is because [the redundancy] is connected with the intermediate time.

Furthermore, because it is appropriate for the opening statement to clearly prescribe the origin [of the rite], and since the other passages serve as commendatory statements (stāvaka) by virtue of that [opening statement], it is not proper to accept a prescription that would entail the postulation of multiple unseen potencies (adṛṣṭa). Moreover—
When a connection with the sacrifice to Viṣṇu and others has been established, the sacrifice would exist by implication;
however, it is not appropriate for this [implication] to occur when [the sacrifice] is already present in the Vedic revelation (śruti) as a subordinate element.

The suffix *tavya* arising from the verbal root *kṛ* (to do) has sacrifice as its subordinate element and Viṣṇu and others as its primary referent; in that case, one would have to conceptually extract the duty to perform the sacrifice from its context and apply it [to Viṣṇu]. However, this is not tenable, because the expression "he sacrifices in between" (*antarā yajati*) possesses a direct formal correspondence [with the original sacrifice]. Thus, by the principle of modification of the name—just as in the case of the terms *darśapūrṇamāsa*—there is a cognition of the archetypal rite.

And [it would follow that it is] subordinate. For when an injunction is understood as being primarily concerned with the connection to Viṣṇu and others, the sacrifice to be enjoined would be the primary element by virtue of its being the object of the injunction, whereas [Viṣṇu] would be subordinate by virtue of being expressed [as a qualifier]. If this were so, it would have to be transitive, like the sentence "he leads the goat to the village."

Because the teaching of the primary [sacrifice] is established. In that case, even if there were separate sentences connected with Viṣṇu and others, they would nevertheless enjoin a deity for that very sacrifice prescribed in the interval, and not establish other distinct rites. Furthermore, the deity is not properly denoted by such [expressions]. For these do not express either the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) or the status of being a deity; what then?

In that case, since the words [denoting the deity] express a substance (dravya) with the action (karman) as a subordinate factor, the second case ending (dvitīyā) must be understood there by making the objective potency (karmaśakti) predominant; however, the status of being a deity (devatātva) is not established by that alone. For, because the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) has the sense of relinquishing (*tyāga*), in the ultimate sense, it is the very substance being relinquished that constitutes the object (karman). Consequently, the deity, being the recipient of that [substance], becomes the object (karman) only subsequently.

It is accomplished. In that context, when there is the possibility of two objects (*karman*), by the maxim "the completion [of the action] is the meaning of the word," the previously relinquished object is concealed and the subsequent object of worship is manifested; thus, by determining that there is only one object, the designation occurs as "he sacrifices to Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇuṃ yajati*) or "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to" (*viṣṇur yaṣṭavyaḥ*), having indeed suppressed the inherent power of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). In that context, the status of being a deity is not explicitly stated; rather, it is determined through implication, characterized by the fact that the nature of the action would otherwise be inexplicable. Now, one might object: since the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) consists essentially in the worship of a deity, the terms "its object" (*karma*) and "deity" (*devatā*) are synonyms, and thus it should not be said that the deity is understood through implication. This is not so, for the word does not directly denote the worship of a deity. Why?
For even praise, because it is a form of worship, can be expressed by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice);
nor will it be said that this [praise] is not an object of worship, as is the case with a guest.

Or else, having superposed the state of being the object (*āpyamānatva*) residing in the act of directing onto the act of relinquishment as well, the entire sacrifice is treated as the object (*karman*).

It is not so stated. Therefore, where there is an indication of the status of recipient (*saṃpradāna*), this is what is meant: "One should relinquish the substance with that [recipient] as the aim, in order to bring about a state of ownership for another. Where there is an indication of the object (*karman*), the meaning there is: "One should designate the deity while relinquishing the substance. And thus, in cases involving the mere act of designation, devoid of the act of relinquishing, there occurs the injunction "sacrifice" (*yajeta*).

Both of these [definitions] are based on secondary indication (*lākṣaṇika*). Even so, the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) is more primary because it is never absent from the element of relinquishment (*tyāga*).

Thus, it has been stated that there is no primary status as a recipient (*sampradāna*); however, he says "and it is also seen" to show that a secondary [status] is indeed observed. It has been stated that even a thousand meanings can be accomplished by a single effort; to this, it is replied:
"Even if a single *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is connected with multiple words, it is nevertheless not enjoined by suffixes that do not repeat."

For it is by means of the case-ending that the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is conveyed. And where there is a single [word], such as *agnīṣoma*, the operation of the suffix occurs only once. However, where even a single *kāraka* is expressed by multiple words connected with different case-endings—as in this very instance, "to Agni and to Prajāpati"—there is a simultaneous consideration [of them].

Because of their existence, Agni and Prajāpati must necessarily be perceived as distinct by the suffix; for the case-ending indeed employs a suffix for the perception of the word-meanings, and it does not employ one for those that are not uttered separately—thus there would be the consequence of repetition. Therefore, this is not a valid solution; so it is stated, even in these two sentences.

Prajāpati alone is enjoined [as the deity]. As for Agni and Sūrya, however, their attainment occurs solely from the wording of the mantra; they are not enjoined by another sentence as deities of that mantra. Since those two deities are already established by those [mantras], they are mentioned in the injunction of Prajāpati for the purpose of praise, according to propriety. Furthermore, regarding the principle "that which is like it is a separate scriptural statement" (*tatprakhyaṃ cānyaśāstram*).

When this statement from [Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.2.34] is cited here, it should be understood as being for the purpose of indicating that [the meaning] is already obtained through the wording of the mantra itself. In this way, there will be no redundancy between the mantra and the injunction (*vidhi*). Otherwise, one would face excessive difficulty in resorting to any one of the following: [the view that it is] an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to avoid the fault of an injunction having its own object already established by another scriptural text (*tadarthaśāstra*), or [that it serves as] a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*), an exclusionary injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*), or the like.

Therefore, it is established that there is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) in that case. As for the claim that there is no cognition of the two evening and morning oblations as parts [of a whole], this should be understood as being due to the recognition of the repetition of the entire ritual, as in the case of the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* and other such rites. It might follow that the *agnihotra* should be offered either in the morning or not at both times; however, this is not the case. Because of the injunction for one's "entire life" (*yāvaj-jīva*), as long as one lives, once the evening offering has been made, the morning time exists while one is still living, and thus the complete set of causal conditions (*nimitta*) arises.
Moreover, that [recipient-hood] is a single entity, and since it is the meaning of the suffix, it is the primary factor. And therefore—

In which sentence is that which is qualified by both understood through the observation of the operation of two words, so that it is enjoined by a single effort? And from that injunction, there follows the implication of the qualifiers exactly as they are perceived. And that [implication] occurs where, as in the case of *agnīṣoma* and the like, there is a single case-ending; here, by virtue of the meaning, there is the status of being a factor (*kāraka*) in the form of a collective whole (*samāhāra*). It is not [otherwise].

The intention here is that even for multiple [factors] such as genus (*jāti*), gender (*liṅga*), and number (*saṃkhyā*)—which are not compounded and are expressed by a single case-ending—it is desired that a rule (*vidhi*) apply when they are conveyed by a single word. The phrase "the case-ending of the factor" (*kāraka-vibhakti*) is used because a rule operates upon what is presented by the word; since its nature is to have action (*kriyā*) as its object, this is a placement within the action.

That [act] is the *upanayana*, and it is expressed by the case-inflection (*kāraka-vibhakti*). Therefore, the two operations of the case-inflection are prompted by the injunctive suffix (*vidhi-pratyaya*); this is the reading found in the Kāśī edition.

Because a secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) is not resorted to without a reason; for a word functions in a secondary sense only when there is a clear grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with another word and when no other possibility exists. Yet neither of these two conditions is present here, for it is possible [to take the word in its primary sense].

The primary animal (*mukhyapaśu*) and the *soma* substance are intended to enjoin another sacrifice. Nor is it the case that these two terms are untenable when not applied to the original sacrifices. Therefore, even if the sacrifices enjoined by the verbs *avadyati* (cuts off) and *gṛhṇāti* (takes), were [already] established, there would still be the consequence of them being distinct rites (*karmāntaratva*). Why? Because in those very sacrifices which require their own respective materials as the source (*prakṛti*), the animal and the *soma* are not enjoined.
Regarding this, it is said: "For by direct scriptural statement (śruti), the juice belongs to Indra and Vāyu.
First of all, since the sentence is intent upon enjoining a deity, it is impossible to enjoin the animal itself when there is no original productive statement (utpattivākya).

It is not even proposed [as an alternative]. Even the *soma* creeper, though enjoined by the sentence, is not connected when there is a conflict with what is directly stated (*śruta*). If it is argued that [the reason] is "because it is seen," then it is unestablished (*asiddha*) because it is merely a part of the proposition (*pratijñātārtha*). Or, if it is [argued] by way of similarity—

It is said thus from his perspective; however, [the author] himself will later refute this.

We do not say that it is illogical for a single thing to have two purposes. We do not deny the inherent capacity of a thing; rather, even though the thing is capable, since its performance has not been enjoined [as having both purposes], curd must necessarily be enjoined as serving both purposes. But this is not possible, because enjoining multiple relationships would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). This is because [the relationship] with the proximate [element] is impossible...

By that [injunction], a remote object is prescribed. Therefore, in this case, if both the connection between the curd and the oblation—which is proximate—and the connection between the curd and the fruit—which is remote—were to be prescribed simultaneously, one would have to accept both possibility and impossibility at once.
Consequently, since one of the two must be abandoned, your position is established; thus, by virtue of the proximate [connection], the curd [is connected to the oblation].
Since that [fire] is also connected with the oblation and with the fruit, when the fruit is joined with the ritual action, the status of being a distinct rite is established.
Indeed, it is understood from the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* that in such sentences, the fruit [of the action] arises from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). How so?
Because the power of the injunction (*vidhisāmarthya*) has not yet been extracted away from the meaning of the verbal root.
In the meantime, it is understood that the connection with the fruit belongs to the meaning of the verbal root.

As for the declaration of a fruit that occurs in connection with one who is endowed with the observance of qualities, that [declaration] is touched by the injunction pertaining to those qualities; therefore, it forms a single syntactical unit with them.

The status of being an injunction (*vidhitva*) resides precisely in the *bhāvanā*, and it migrates from one place to another according to the difference in its purpose. When the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) reaches that stage of migration where the *bhāvanā* possesses a fruit, then it makes the very meaning of the verbal root the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Furthermore, it becomes for the sake of that [fruit]. And this occurs in such cases as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice."

Because a noun is incapable of subverting the power of an injunction (*vidhi-śakti*), [the injunction] remains unobstructed. However, in this case, the word "curd" (*dadhi*), being untouched by any of the characteristics of a name, must necessarily effect an injunction; thus, it rescues the injunctive force that had fallen upon the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

Consequently, when the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)—colored by the curd—is found to be dependent on the verbal root’s meaning as its required correlate (*ākāṅkṣita*), the result (*phala*) is perceived therein.

It is determined that [the rice] is a means for producing curds (*dadhi*), not a means for the oblation (*homa*). For we do not accept the claim that "since unenjoined matters are disregarded, the action initiated by those [means] accomplishes its result through the very nature of the substance, such as rice (*vrīhi*)"; this is because even if one intended [to argue] that it is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*), that was not understood in the preceding treatise.

To one who thinks, "He says this because it consists of the power of the objective entity (*vastu-sāmarthya-mayam*)," the following reply is given: "We do not say so. Therefore, this explanation is common to both positions. [The phrase] "the connection with the fruit occurs in the quality" refers to this:
that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as required by the context. In this regard, if the meaning of the verbal root—

Since it is designated as a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is non-difference only of that [the sacrifice], not of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*). How, then, is there no separate action? Or how is it that there is no injunction of multiple connections by means of the prior efficient force? Now, according to the reading printed in Kāśī, [it is argued that] even for the efficient force, the purpose of both is to be the means of accomplishing the fruit.

Thus it has been stated. And just as there is no injunction for the *homa* (oblation) because the injunction is implied by the word "curd" (*dadhi*), so too there is no injunction of curd for the *homa* upon considering the word expressing the result. What then? [The injunction applies] to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) toward the result. Therefore, the result belongs to the curd.
Which word here expresses the human effort (*puruṣaprayatna*)? Since neither the word "curd" nor the word "result-producer" denotes the *bhāvanā*, [the effort is expressed by the verbal suffix].

The question arises from the perspective of one who considers that, since it is impossible for the root-meaning itself to be the direct object of an injunction (*vidhi*), and because the application [of the word] depends upon the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*)— as stated in *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 2.1.4— and thus one is unable to abandon the root-meaning, the result must arise from the root-meaning itself. The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*), however, [holds that] the suffix has the nature of an injunction and the root-meaning has the nature of a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Seeing it as divided, he says: "one should sacrifice. Now, the opponent’s own intention is explained: [the word] "this" is connected to the oblation by virtue of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). And human effort is called *bhāvanā* when accompanied by an injunction. True; this has been relied upon elsewhere precisely because of the superior force of direct scriptural statement according to the principle of the section on the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*). And here, those who hold your position—

In that very way, its true nature (tattva) is stated. Likewise, although there is a difference in the results of the injunctions for obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites, and although there is a diversity of functions conditioned by those results, because the underlying continuity in the form of the cognition of the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is indeed a conventional usage of non-difference; so it is elsewhere as well.

For instance, in the injunction "one offers the Agnihotra," there is a description of the activity as being the subject matter of this sentence without specifying a particular type of oblation; likewise, in the sentence concerning one who desires sense organs (*indriyakāma*), having taken up that same verbal meaning (*ākhyātārtha*) with the addition of curd (*dadhi*), the addition of the result is then taken up. Therefore, there is no subversion of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

Furthermore, the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) does not have the status of a subordinate member (*aṅga*) with respect to the objecthood (*karmatva*) of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), because that [objecthood] is delimited by a connection common to the factors of object, instrument, and so forth, as understood through the direct denotation of the word (*padaśruti*). How then will this be stated: "in order to enjoin a *bhāvanā* qualified by curd and the sense-faculty"?
And how [can it be said that] when the *bhāvanā* is already established [by another injunction], [the result and the means are enjoined] by means of the context and the syntactical connection?

If it is argued that there is the presentation of two types of relationship, the refutation will occur at the conclusion of this section: "The injunction is colored by the result. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are first enjoined as optional alternatives, each serving as a means for the *pṛṣṭha* stotra;

Regarding the passage, "If [the sacrifice] has the Bṛhat-sāman, [it should have] the Śukra-vessels first," a doubt arises concerning the ritual action (karman) heard there as being endowed with attributes:

Is this a separate ritual action from the Jyotiṣṭoma, or is it merely a scriptural statement intended to establish a specific rule regarding the precedence of the vessels for that very same [Jyotiṣṭoma], contingent upon its being delimited by the Rathantara-sāman? Therefore, for the sake of establishing this point, the following investigation is undertaken.
One must consider whether this connection with the *kratu* (sacrifice) pertains to the *rathantara* [sāman] in its entirety, or merely to its existence.

For the sake of establishing that point, this too must be deliberated: is it the *rathantara* as qualified by the sacrifice that is intended here, or is it the sacrifice as qualified by the *rathantara*? But surely, because of the connection with the word "if" (*yadi*), a condition (*nimitta*) is perceived here; and that [condition] is to be designated—

Because it would be a mere injunction (*māna*), the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) would not be possible. This [term] could serve as a conditional cause (*nimittārthatva*) only if it were understood that such a thing—as this [quality] is perceived—were obtained from some other source. However, in the case where it is not so obtained, it necessarily results in an injunction (*vidhāna*). It might be argued that [the word] has the purpose of indicating a characteristic (*nimitta*). An injunction (*vidhi*) is accepted. Therefore, when the meaning of the term *rathantarasāman* is examined, if it is understood as already established [by another rule], then its status as a condition (*nimittatā*) follows the established doctrine; however, in the absence of such establishment, if an injunction is reached through the abandonment of the word and so forth, and not by way of connection with a qualifier, then it is indeed a condition. And that [springtime], being connected with the performance-injunction (*prayoga-vidhi*), takes up the action. If that [action] is supplied by the context (*prakaraṇa*), then...

Quite so. Even when a sentence does not conclude with a mere restatement, the granting of that [status] does not bring excessive fault; thus, "by means of that, one becomes a Brāhmaṇa who is establishing [the fires]. If there were a connection between the two words "if" (*yadi*) and "Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇaḥ*), then it would have the sense of being a condition (*nimitta*); this is the intent of the Bhāṣya. In that case, because there is no connection between the two grammatical factors (*kāraka*), they are brought into relation through their connection with a single action.

He says, "And then," because the lineage (*anvaya*) is the result, as it is the object of the word’s intended meaning (*śabdatātparya*). By this [he means] "in the spring. Since the injunctions for the performance of rituals imply the study of the Veda as the means for knowing them, [the lineage] is not brought about [by those injunctions].
